result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.get_label_from_id()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Get the label for a node by its ID. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L6890-L6968){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.get_label_from_id(node_id) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Label from id](/assets/graphs/get-label-from-id.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="The shared four-node graph with node ids in pills. The queried id 2 is highlighted, and the node it belongs to, B, is filled in the accent color. The card returns the label B." width="100%"} Translates an internal `u64` node ID to its human-readable string label. Returns `None` if the node doesn't exist or has no label assigned. Many methods return node IDs -- `get_node_ids()`, `neighbors()`, shortest paths, and the dictionaries from centrality and community methods with `return_dict=True` -- so this is the usual way to make such results readable. A common idiom is a comprehension like `{graph.get_label_from_id(nid): value for nid, value in result.items()}`. `get_id_from_label()` does the reverse translation. The method never raises. Keep in mind that `None` is ambiguous: it is returned both for IDs that aren't in the graph and for nodes that exist but have no label (as with nodes made by random generators like `add_gnp_graph()`). Use `get_node()` if you need to tell the two cases apart. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [node_id]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The integer node ID to look up, as returned by `get_node_ids()`, `get_id_from_label()`, and similar methods. Values that aren't valid IDs return `None`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The string label if it exists, or `None` if the node has no label or doesn't exist in the graph. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} This is the inverse of `get_id_from_label()`, translating an internal ID back to its label: ::: {#27e5978a .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["Alice", "Bob", "Carol"]) .add_edges([("Alice", "Bob"), ("Bob", "Carol")]) ) graph.get_label_from_id(1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 'Alice' ``` ::: ::: A node ID that doesn't exist returns `None`: ::: {#c0a54c88 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.get_label_from_id(999) ``` ::: Results keyed by node ID become much easier to read once the IDs are swapped for labels: ::: {#804444f7 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} scores = graph.betweenness_centrality(return_dict=True) {graph.get_label_from_id(nid): score for nid, score in scores.items()} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` {'Alice': 0.0, 'Carol': 0.0, 'Bob': 1.0} ``` ::: ::: Nodes created without a label also return `None`, even though they exist. Random generators such as `add_gnp_graph()` create unlabelled nodes: ::: {#a4e52477 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} random_graph = ec.Graph().add_gnp_graph(n=3, p=0.5, seed=1) random_graph.get_label_from_id(1), random_graph.get_node(1) is not None ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` (None, True) ``` ::: :::
